awd_titl_txt: Travel: RI: NSF Student Travel Grant for 2025 IEEE International Conference on Computational Photography (ICCP)
awd_abstract_narration:
This award supports the participation of students from U.S.-based institutions in the IEEE International Conference on Computational Photography (ICCP) 2025, taking place in person from July 19–23, 2025, at the University of Toronto in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Now in its seventeenth year, ICCP is the premier annual conference dedicated to computational photography, bringing together researchers from optics, image and signal processing, computer vision and graphics, and sensor and electronics communities. The ICCP 2025 program features keynote and invited talks, technical paper presentations, poster and demo sessions, and networking opportunities—fostering interdisciplinary collaboration and providing an engaging environment for both junior and senior researchers to exchange ideas and mentorship.

This award offers travel grants to 20 U.S.-based students, selected through a competitive process by a committee of ICCP 2025 organizers. Grants will partially cover travel, lodging, and registration expenses. Selected students are expected to fully participate in the ICCP program—including all talks, poster/demo sessions, and networking events—and will present their own research in a poster session. They will also take part in a mentoring event with academic and industry professionals offering guidance on research and career development. Additionally, recipients will attend the inaugural ICCP Summer School on Computational Imaging, featuring lectures by leading experts on active research topics in the field. Participation in ICCP 2025 will support students’ professional growth, enhance their research skills, and offer valuable networking opportunities. This initiative aims to strengthen the future STEM workforce by encouraging students to pursue careers in science and engineering, while simultaneously enriching the broader computational photography and computing research communities. Ultimately, this program contributes to increasing the number of active researchers and educators in STEM, thereby advancing the development of impactful technologies for society.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award helped create the ICCP Summer School on Computational Imaging and establish it as a permanent component of the IEEE International Conference on Computational Photography (ICCP). The inaugural school took place as a two-day event during ICCP 2025 at the University of Toronto in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The school was attended by 25 competitively selected undergraduate and graduate students. Among these students, 20 were from U.S.-based universities, and this award provided travel grants to support their attendance at both the summer school and the main ICCP conference.

ICCP is organized with the vision of fostering a community of researchers who converge on computational photography, despite traditionally coming from distinct disciplines, including imaging and optics; image and signal processing; computer vision and graphics; and sensors and electronics. Topics typically featured in the conference include computational cameras, computational displays, computational illumination and optics, novel and advanced sensor design, high-performance and scientific imaging, advanced signal processing methods, augmented and virtual reality, optical computing, and microscopy. In 2025, ICCP was in its seventeenth year. Over the previous decade, it built a dedicated community of around 300 regular participants across computer vision, computer graphics, signal processing, imaging and optics, and sensors and electronics.

Intellectual Merit. The funds provided by this award fully covered ICCP 2025 attendance costs—including registration, travel, accommodation, and meals—for 20 students from U.S.-based institutions (approximately 10% of total attendees). Half of the supported students were undergraduates and half were graduate students.

The students attended the inaugural ICCP Summer School on Computational Imaging. The school featured courses on cutting-edge research topics in computational imaging, taught by world-class instructors and emphasizing hands-on software and hardware skills. The courses covered black hole imaging (instructor: Katie Bouman, Caltech), virtual reality headsets (instructor: Gordon Wetzstein, Stanford), single-photon imaging (instructor: Mohit Gupta, University of Wisconsin–Madison), and interferometric imaging (instructor: Ioannis Gkioulekas, Carnegie Mellon University).

Participating students learned how to use data from the Event Horizon Telescope to reconstruct images of black holes, and built prototype VR headsets, single-photon LiDAR systems, and white-light interferometers. The award helped establish the school as a permanent part of ICCP, with plans already underway for the second iteration of the summer school at ICCP 2026.

Besides the summer school, students had the opportunity to participate in all aspects of the main ICCP conference, including talks from the paper program, keynote talks, invited talks, the poster session, the demo session, the awards session, and social events (banquet, photography competition).

Broader Impacts. The student travel grants provided through this award helped increase undergraduate and graduate student participation at ICCP. The award supported students from research groups and research areas that do not traditionally participate in the conference, as well as students who did not have alternative funding resources for attendance. Thus, the award facilitated cross-pollination of ideas across research communities and helped advance science.

The ICCP Summer School on Computational Imaging created through this award directly contributes to next-generation workforce development in the United States by encouraging participating students to pursue research and STEM careers and by equipping them with research skills and networking opportunities for success in such careers. By enabling their participation in the main ICCP conference, the summer school provides undergraduate and graduate students with exposure to a truly interdisciplinary research area, a high-profile venue to present their research, and opportunities to form connections with mentors and peers across academia and industry.

Feedback solicited from participating students in the form of testimonials and outcome reports will be used by the ICCP steering committee to continue and expand the summer school and strengthen its contributions to broadening engagement and participation in STEM.
